newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Rand exposes S.Africa woes, but is gloom overdone?.
newsitem.headline: Rand exposes S.Africa woes, but is gloom overdone?.

text.p: The recent run on the rand highlights economic problems facing post-apartheid South Africa, but analysts say many fundamentals remain sound and the all-important balance of payments will improve in 1997.
Low foreign reserves and a protracted current account deficit are the central problems exposed by the rand's 30 percent slide against the dollar this year.

The two are clearly linked -- until the balance of payments improves reserves will stay low, the rand will be vulnerable to speculative attacks and capital outflows will continue, depleting reserves further in a vicious circle.
Uncertainty about how and when exchange controls on residents will be lifted has only exacerbated the problem, as investors try to second-guess a move that could trigger a further capital flight.
Yet by international standards South Africa is hardly a basket case.
According to Dave Mohr, chief economist at leading life assurer Old Mutual, the balance of payments deficit is quite modest at three percent of gross domestic product.
"The deficit only needs to be narrowed moderately, say to about half its present size, in order to match the present lower level of capital inflows," he said on Thursday.
While the government clearly had to do more to inspire confidence -- notably by a firm commitment to privatisation -- the fundamental problems facing the new South Africa should not be exaggerated.
Other analysts agreed the trade balance would correct as a weak rand and high interest rates curbed imports and boosted exports.

It won't happen overnight. Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals warned earlier this week that the current account deficit would remain large at around 12 billion rand ($2.55 billion) in 1996, little changed from 12.7 billion in 1995.
But analysts are confident it will turn eventually.

Swiss bank UBS, whose bearish report in February contributed to the initial fall in the rand, expects the visible trade surplus to jump from $1.4 billion this year to $2.4 billion in 1997, going a long way to offset a deficit in services.
"That should support the rand recovery over the coming months," the bank said in a note to clients, predicting the currency would outperform inflation differentials in 1997.
The last serious rand crash was in 1985, when the central bank closed the foreign exchange market and imposed a moratorium on the repayments of international commitments.

But economists said conditions today were very different. Then commodity prices were slumping, the outside world was tightening sanctions on apartheid South Africa and political violence was mounting.
In 1996, political violence is largely a thing of the past -- although violent crime is a major problem -- and metal prices, though weak, have not slumped as they did in the mid-1980s.

As a result, Mohr is confident that South Africa can adjust its balance of payments without throwing the economy into recession, even if there has to be a short-term hike in already punitive interest rates.
He predicts economic growth will slow from 3.3 percent in 1996 to two percent in 1997, but accelerate again in 1998.
